rows.say: MintMismatch happens when you're using TransferChecked and the mint account you pass doesn't match the one associated with the token account. The checked variant validates that the mint address is correct, whereas the unchecked Transfer instruction skips this safety check.

rows.say: NonNativeHasBalance means you tried to close a token account for a non-wrapped token that still has a balance; the token balance must be zero before closing. Wrapped SOL is the exception—you can close a wSOL account even with SOL in it.

rows.say: A blockhash becomes too old if enough time passes between fetching it and submitting your transaction, or if your RPC node is lagging behind the network. Use finalized blockhashes and submit quickly, or retry with a fresh blockhash if the network has moved on.

rows.say: The Solana transaction pipeline says this error means the network already processed and cached your transaction — it went through once, so the network rejects it again to protect you from double-spending. Don't resend the exact same transaction; if you retry, use a fresh blockhash.

If you're sending to a new account, that adds a one-time account setup fee of about 0.002 SOL. A common mistake: you have enough SOL in total, but not enough after accounting for rent-exempt minimums on existing accounts.

rows.say: Proof of History proves that an event happened before another event and that time actually passed: the next hash must be produced sequentially from the previous one and transaction IDs are hashed into the stream, creating an unforgeable chain of events. A common trap is thinking it proves ownership or validity of transactions—it doesn't, it just establishes order and elapsed time.

rows.say: Turbine spreads a block by cutting it into shreds, sending each shred to a small set of validators, and then those validators pass it on down a tree — so no one has to send the whole block to everyone. This way the network doesn't get bogged down.

rows.say: Solana doesn't have a mempool like Ethereum does. Transactions are processed immediately by validators from a single network path, with no queue stage where users compete on gas fees — that's the old Ethereum belief. The transaction pipeline validates and executes sequentially, and priority fees are used only to influence which packets are selected when the network is congested.

sources.title: Transaction Pipeline

rows.say: Sealevel runs transactions in parallel by having each transaction declare which accounts it reads and writes up front, so the scheduler can run any two transactions that do not write the same account at the same time. Two transactions that both want to write to the same account run one after the other. A common belief that is out of date: that Solana runs all transactions in parallel with no limits.

sources.title: How the network runs — slots, consensus, clients, as of 2026-09
sources.source: Anza docs and the Solana Improvement Documents

rows.say: Solana processes transactions that write to the same account sequentially, not in parallel, so only one can run at a time. This is because the validator needs to order them to avoid conflicts — if two tried to modify the same data at once, the results would be unpredictable. A common trap is thinking this is a bottleneck: good program design avoids write-locking a single account, spreading writes across accounts so transactions can run in parallel.

sources.title: JSON Reference

rows.say: On Solana, priority fees are worked out per account, not across the whole chain — so competition to write one hot account raises fees only for that account, leaving unrelated transactions cheap. That is a local fee market: one busy mint does not make a plain transfer expensive, which is why Solana does not have a single network-wide gas price like other chains.

rows.say: A Geyser plugin is a shared library a validator loads to stream account writes, transactions, blocks and other data into a database or websocket feed — that's how indexers and RPC providers keep up without constantly polling. It has nothing to do with Minecraft; on Solana it's the validator's plugin interface defined by the agave-geyser-plugin-interface crate.

rows.say: A snapshot is a compressed copy of all accounts on Solana at a specific slot, used by validators to start up quickly without replaying the whole blockchain from the beginning. Snapshots are also useful for analytics to load account data fast.

rows.say: Firedancer is an independent validator client written from scratch by Jump Crypto, as of September 2026. Full Firedancer went live on mainnet in December 2025 and now runs about 14% of the network's stake, alongside Frankendancer (a hybrid using Firedancer's networking with Agave's runtime) at about 26%. It was never testnet-only — that's stale documentation.

rows.say: The Solana validator earns rewards from network inflation based on its vote credits each epoch; at epoch end, those rewards are automatically deposited into delegators' stake accounts, minus the validator's commission. Rewards are calculated from the validator's performance, not claimed manually.

rows.say: A validator votes on every slot it agrees with, and each vote is a transaction that costs SOL in fees — roughly 1 SOL a day at current slot times. Stake rewards from the validator's vote credits are meant to cover this cost, but a validator with too little stake pays more in votes than it earns.

The original Token program has none of these. A trap: Token-2022 won't show in some tools yet, so check your wallet supports what you need.

rows.say: signAndSendTransactions signs a transaction and sends it to the network in one call, returning a signature once it's submitted. It replaces the older signTransactions method, which only signed without sending. The wallet handles the submission to the chain, so your app doesn't have to.

rows.say: Seed Vault is a secure system on the phone that keeps your private keys and secrets locked in the phone's most secure part—its hardware security environment—so they never leave that safe space. When you approve a transaction or sign a message, Seed Vault handles it there and shows you what you're signing, so apps never touch your keys directly. A common trap: you might think the app is signing things, but Seed Vault is the only thing that actually signs.
